passage:
Tejas, listen, it wasn't my fault. I know Mummy always says, 'Vinita, you panic in exams,' but this time, no. Seriously. The maths paper had that whole section on probability that sir never finished in class. Never. Half of it was out of syllabus, I swear. And the invigilator kept walking past my bench, tap tap tap with the pen, I couldn't think.
Also I was sitting right under the broken fan. Bad luck, total bad luck.
No, I haven't told Mummy. She thinks the papers come back next Friday. I'll tell her when the retest thing is sorted, maybe. Or after Diwali.
Which questions did I get wrong? I don't know, I didn't look. I just put the sheet in my bag. Why would I look? It's not like the marks change.
Anyway, can we not talk about it? Let's go get pani puri. My treat. Come on, Tejas.
Why are you looking at me like that?

qa.q: Where did Vinita put the answer sheet?
qa.a: Vinita just put the sheet in the bag without looking at it.

qa.q: Why might Vinita want to change the subject to pani puri?
qa.a: Vinita seems hurt and embarrassed, and talking about the paper feels too painful, so changing the subject is a way to avoid it.

qa.q: What small step could help Vinita get past blaming the paper?
qa.a: Vinita could open the answer sheet with a friend or teacher and look at just a few wrong questions, then tell Mummy before Friday.

qa.q: How might Tejas be feeling while listening to all these reasons?
qa.a: Tejas may notice that the excuses keep changing and feel worried that Vinita is hiding from the result instead of dealing with it.

grounding: It shows a teen blaming the teacher, the paper and bad luck, avoiding telling the parent, and refusing to look at the mistakes.

passage:
I'm Vandana, Payal's didi. I can only tell you what I saw that week.
On Monday Payal came home from school and went straight to the bathroom for a long time. At dinner Mummy asked if the physics unit test papers were back. Payal said, 'Not yet, Ma'am is very slow.'
On Tuesday I saw a folded answer sheet sticking out of the side pocket of her bag. Red ink. I didn't open it.
On Wednesday her friend Kajal called twice on the landline. Payal told me to say she was sleeping. She wasn't.
On Thursday, when I asked lightly how physics was going, she said, 'That teacher marks unfairly, everyone says so. The paper was stupid anyway.'
Maybe it was. I don't know. But she hasn't opened her physics notebook all week, and she used to love that subject.

qa.q: What did Vandana see sticking out of Payal's bag on Tuesday?
qa.a: She saw a folded answer sheet sticking out of the side pocket, with red ink.

qa.q: What might Payal be worried about when she tells Mummy the papers aren't back?
qa.a: Payal may be afraid of disappointing Mummy and ashamed of the mark, so hiding feels safer for now.

qa.q: How could Vandana help Payal at this stage without forcing her?
qa.a: Vandana could tell Payal privately that she noticed, say one bad test is not a big deal to her, and offer to sit with her while she looks at the paper or tells Mummy.

qa.q: How does Vandana see Payal's week?
qa.a: Vandana sees her sister hiding and avoiding things, and she is worried because Payal has stopped even opening a subject she used to love.

grounding: It shows, through a sister's eyes, a teen blaming the teacher and the paper and hiding a bad result from family and friends, which stops her learning.

passage:
Hi Santosh bhaiya,
Don't mention this to anyone at home, okay? The Class 11 half-yearly results came. I failed physics. 19 out of 80.
Honestly it wasn't my fault. The paper was set from chapters sir hadn't even finished, and half the class complained. Plus the invigilator kept walking up and down and I couldn't concentrate.
I didn't even look at the answer sheet when it came back. I just folded it into my bag.
I haven't told Mummy-Papa. The report card has to be signed by Friday, so I'll say the school's printer broke. I told my friends I got 45. Nobody needs to know.
I know you'll say I should talk to sir about the paper. But what's the point, he'll just blame me. It's easier this way. I feel fine now, mostly.
Anyway, how's college? Send photos of the hostel.
Tarun

qa.q: What mark did Tarun get in physics?
qa.a: 19 out of 80.

qa.q: What might Tarun be feeling underneath 'I feel fine now, mostly'?
qa.a: Tarun is likely hurt and anxious about the parents' reaction, and blaming the paper and the invigilator eases the sting for now.

qa.q: What turning point could Santosh offer at this stage?
qa.a: Santosh could reply kindly, urge Tarun to tell Mummy-Papa before Friday, and suggest going through the folded answer sheet with sir to see what actually went wrong.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel reading this email?
qa.a: Santosh may feel trusted but uneasy, caught between keeping the secret and wanting to help Tarun stop hiding.

grounding: A teen blames the paper and the invigilator and hides a failed result from parents and friends, which blocks any learning from it.

passage:
Parveen, don't give me that look. Yes, Jahnavi, who never misses anything, skipped the result meeting yesterday. I had a headache. A real one.
Okay, fine, partly real. You want to know? I got a D in chemistry. A D. But listen, that paper was ridiculous, the questions were nothing like the sample paper, and Ma'am gave the toppers extra hints in the revision class. Everyone saw it.
And no, I haven't told my parents. Mummy thinks the results come next week. If I tell her now she'll cancel the trip to Nani's. What's the use? It won't change the grade.
I haven't even opened the marked paper. It's in my locker, face down.
I just don't want to talk about it. Every time someone asks, my stomach does this twisting thing. So we're not talking about chemistry today. Tell me about your match instead.

qa.q: What grade did Jahnavi get in chemistry?
qa.a: A D in chemistry.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi's twisting stomach reveal about how the grade feels?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels hurt and anxious about the D, and blaming the paper and changing the subject keep that pain at a distance.

qa.q: What would help Jahnavi move past this stage?
qa.a: Telling the parents now and turning over the marked paper with the teacher would make the D something to learn from instead of hide.

qa.q: What is it like for Parveen to hear this?
qa.a: Parveen may feel worried and a bit shut out, since Jahnavi wants company but refuses to talk about what is really hurting.

grounding: A teen blames the paper and the teacher and avoids telling parents, shielding from the hurt but leaving the marked paper unread.

passage:
Monday. The mock board results went up on the notice board. Nitin found his name near the bottom in maths and walked off before Yash could see. At lunch he announced that the checking was rigged; the teacher always marked the back benches harder.
Wednesday. His mother asked at dinner when the results would come. "They got delayed, the teachers are on some training," Nitin said, eyes on his plate. Upstairs he pushed the answer sheet deep inside an old geography textbook without reading the teacher's red notes.
Saturday. Yash texted: "did u check where u lost marks? sir said we can see him monday." Nitin typed "nah bad luck, paper was weird" and turned his phone face down. The parent-teacher meeting was nine days away, and the textbook sat on the shelf as if it were ticking.

qa.q: Where did Nitin hide the answer sheet?
qa.a: Deep inside an old geography textbook.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when he said the results got delayed?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and afraid of his mother's reaction, so lying and blaming the checking protected him from the hurt for now.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Nitin on Saturday?
qa.a: Taking Yash's suggestion to see sir on Monday and reading the red notes would turn the result into something to learn from before the meeting.

qa.q: How might Yash see Nitin's reply about bad luck?
qa.a: Yash probably senses Nitin is avoiding it and may feel concerned, since the offer to look at lost marks got brushed aside.

grounding: Over a week a teen blames the checking and bad luck and hides the result from his mother, which blocks him from learning from it.

passage: "Minakshi, since you won't show your mother the report card, let your Rekha bua tell you what I did at fifteen. I failed the half-yearly maths paper. Twenty-eight out of a hundred. And do you know what I told everyone? The paper was out of syllabus. The teacher hated me. My pen leaked. The fan was too noisy. Each story was a little bit true, and together they made one big lie. I hid the report card inside my geography book for three weeks and told Amma the results weren't out yet. By the finals I had the same gaps, because I had never looked at a single wrong answer. Then my cousin found the card and, instead of shouting, sat with me and went through the paper question by question. That was the first time I learned anything from it."

qa.q: What did young Rekha score in the half-yearly maths paper?
qa.a: Twenty-eight out of a hundred.

qa.q: Why did young Rekha keep blaming the paper, the teacher and the fan?
qa.a: She was ashamed and scared, and blaming others shielded her from the pain of failing.

qa.q: What choice inside the story finally helped?
qa.a: Going through the paper question by question with the cousin, instead of hiding the card, let her learn from what went wrong.

qa.q: What might the cousin have felt on finding the hidden card?
qa.a: The cousin may have been surprised but chose kindness over shouting, wanting to help rather than punish.

grounding: Shows a teen blaming the paper, the teacher and luck and hiding the result from family, which shields from pain but blocks learning.
